FOR 112.subject: FOR
FOR 112.description: An overview of computing applications used in all aspects of forestry work, but largely focused on development of intermediate and advanced spreadsheet skills using Microsoft Excel (e.g., complex formulas and functions, charting, and pivot tables). Additionally, the course rounds out essential skills in document formatting and presentation development.

FOR 206.subject: FOR
FOR 206.description: Explores forest soils in managed and unmanaged ecosystems of the Oregon Willamette Valley and coast range with an emphasis on learning tools to observe, describe and quantify soil chemical and physical properties in the field and the laboratory. Guides students through the scientific process (hypothesis development, sample collection, lab analysis, data analysis and report writing) to investigate potential effects of forest management on local forest soils and their ability to support tree growth. (Core Education or Bacc Core Course if taken with SOIL 205 )
attributes: CFSL – Core Ed - Scientific Inquiry & Analysis Attached Lab ; CPPS – Bacc Core

FOR 208.subject: FOR
FOR 208.description: Readings, exercises, discussions designed to develop student competency in forest soil processes, description, analysis, and assessment. A particular emphasis will be placed on the role of soils in managed and unmanaged forest ecosystems.

FOR 210.subject: FOR
FOR 210.course_name: TERRESTRIAL VERTEBRATE IDENTIFICATION AND NATURAL HISTORY
FOR 210.description: Reviews principles used for locating, observing, and identifying terrestrial vertebrates, with an emphasis on using morphological characteristics in concert with behaviors and vegetation associations. Emphasizes on taxonomic relationships and traits used for identifying species within each terrestrial vertebrate group (i.e., birds, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals). Gains experience in species identification under field conditions and explores the relationship between animals and their environments.
FOR 210.recommended: One term or year of introductory biology

FOR 252.subject: FOR
FOR 252.description: Builds solid foundation in wildland firefighting and basic fire behavior. Incorporates National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) online curricula. Develops firefighting skills, including fire shelter deployment and a Work Capacity Test (WCT) opportunity, through a series of field-based exercises.

FOR 253.subject: FOR
FOR 253.description: Emphasizes basic, but essential, concepts related to the health, well-being, and safety of firefighters working in the demanding wildland environment.

FOR 300X.subject: FOR
FOR 300X.course_name: DEALING WITH STRESS IN WILDLAND FIRE
FOR 300X.description: Provides detailed information on the nature and effects of stress and burnout in personal and work settings. Covers the history of stress management research and the development of effective stress management programs. Uses simple stress measurement tools to assess stress. Explores the causes and effects of general stress, cumulative stress, critical incident stress, and the conditions resulting from exposure to trauma events. Emphasizes practical steps to control stress reactions by means of practical and reliable stress control methods.

FOR 312.subject: FOR
FOR 312.description: A hands-on experience in the major aspects of forestry, including regeneration surveys, silviculture, cruising, recreation, forest disturbances, logging site and mill visits, east and west of the Cascades Range. CROSSLISTED as FE 312 / FOR 312 .

FOR 321.subject: FOR
FOR 321.description: Encompasses methods used to measure tree, stand and forest-level attributes, and sample and analyze forest resources data. Provides information that support forest management decisions at the stand and forest levels. Focuses mainly on quantitative analysis of forest vegetation. Uses considerable time and effort on measuring other forest resources (e.g., wildlife habitat and riparian zones).
FOR 321.prerequisites_raw: FES 241 with C or better and FE 208 [C] and ( MTH 241 [C] or MTH 245 [C] or MTH 251Z [C] or MTH 251HZ [C] or MTH 251 [C] or MTH 251H [C]) and (ST 201 [C] or ST 243Z [C] or ST 314 [C] or ST 351 [C])

FOR 322.subject: FOR
FOR 322.description: Focuses on introduction to static and dynamic forest models: defining what they are, how they might be used, and, in general terms, how they are developed.
FOR 322.prerequisites_raw: FOR 321 with C or better and ( MTH 241 [C] or MTH 241H [C] or MTH 251Z [C] or MTH 251HZ [C] or MTH 251 [C] or MTH 251H [C]) and (ST 201 [C] or ST 243Z [C] or ST 314 [C] or ST 351 [C])

FOR 329.subject: FOR
FOR 329.description: Explores main concepts associated with the sustainable use of forest resources from an economic perspective. Introduces financial and economic aspects of forest management decision making, at both the stand and forest level. Topics including forest products markets, appraisal, rotation, thinning, uneven-aged management and forest regulation. Covers economics of timber management and harvest scheduling.
FOR 329.prerequisites_raw: ST 201 with C or better or ST 243Z with C or better or ST 314 with C or better or ST 314H with C or better or ST 351 with C or better or ST 351H with C or better

FOR 332.subject: FOR
FOR 332.description: Utilizes tools of investment analysis and approaches to capital budgeting under risk. Explores basic wood products markets. Examines forest resource market failures and externalities. Evaluates nonmarket valuation and multiple-use forestry. Discusses impacts of forest management and public policy decisions on forest resource use. Analyzes international trade considerations.

FOR 346.subject: FOR
FOR 346.description: An interdisciplinary survey of concepts relating to fire science, ecology, management, and policy. Includes case studies of several representative ecosystems, ranging from west- and eastside forests of the Pacific Northwest to shrub steppe ecosystems of the Intermountain West and chaparral ecosystems of southern California. Distance and campus-based delivery using videos, website, and discussion.
FOR 346.recommended: Coursework in forest biology or ecology (eg. FOR 240 or FES 240 or FES 341 )

FOR 410.subject: FOR
FOR 410.description: Full-time supervised professional experience emphasizing functional proficiency under joint sponsorship of university and agency personnel.

FOR 413.subject: FOR
FOR 413.description: Analyzes effects of diseases on forest ecosystems. Focuses on recognition of important groups, prediction of pathogen responses to environmental changes, and management strategies for protection of forest resources. CROSSLISTED as BOT 413 / FOR 413 .
FOR 413.prerequisites_raw: BI 204 with C or better or BI 221Z with C or better or BI 221HZ with C or better or BI 221 with C or better or BI 221H with C or better or BI 213 with C or better or BI 213H with C or better or FES 240 with C or better

FOR 431.subject: FOR
FOR 431.course_name: ECONOMICS AND POLICY OF FOREST WILDLAND FIRE
FOR 431.description: Explores current issues in wildfire policy and management. Analyzes relevant laws and regulations, including liability standards and air quality rules. Uses an economic framework for evaluating allocation of resources, the role of incentives and risk preferences, and for valuation of forest assets under risk.
FOR 431.prerequisites_raw: FOR 330 with C or better or FOR 332 with C or better or ECON 201Z with C or better or ECON 201HZ with C or better or ECON 201 with C or better or ECON 201H with C or better or AEC 250 with C or better or AEC 250H with C or better

FOR 436.subject: FOR
FOR 436.description: Principles and applications of fire as a natural resource management tool; the role of fire in conservation management, restoration, and preservation of ecosystems. Covers basic techniques and current research used to describe fire behavior and spread, fuels and fuel manipulation, and fire effects on the biota. Focus will be on fire as a natural process in ecosystem dynamics.

FOR 438.subject: FOR
FOR 438.description: Emphasizes wildfire impacts to social and ecological values and conducts an assessment of wildfire risk to communities and wildlands. Explores mitigation opportunities from the built environment to wildlands, and how decision-makers use decision-support tools to prioritize actions. Identifies and critiques competing perspectives of risk, from defining the problem to implementing solutions. Applies gained knowledge to real-world examples to reinforce complexities of addressing wildfire risk.

FOR 441.subject: FOR
FOR 441.description: Nursery operation, vegetation management, herbivores, fire, seeding and planting techniques. Introduction to principles and techniques involving vegetation control, thinning, fertilizing, and harvesting. Environmental considerations related to forest stand treatments.
FOR 441.prerequisites_raw: ( FES 240 with C or better or FES 240H with C or better) and FES 241 [C]

FOR 442.subject: FOR
FOR 442.description: Silvicultural principles and practices needed to successfully regenerate forestlands in North America. Topics include artificial and natural regeneration, genetic improvement, seed orchards, forest tree nurseries, site preparation, seedling quality and handling, vegetation management, animal damage protection, early stand management, and ecological and ecophysiological considerations. Emphasis is placed on regeneration methods applied to plantations in western Oregon. Field trips required.
FOR 442.prerequisites_raw: ( SOIL 205 with C or better or SOIL 205H with C or better or CSS 205 with C or better or CSS 305 with C or better) and ( FES 240 [C] or FES 240H [C])

FOR 443.subject: FOR
FOR 443.description: Manipulation of forest stand structure and dynamics to meet various resource management objectives. Covers key concepts and practices associated with vegetation control, thinning, fertilization, even-aged and uneven-aged regeneration systems including social and environmental considerations associated with treatments. Two-day field trip required.
FOR 443.prerequisites_raw: ( FES 240 with C or better or FES 240H with C or better) and FOR 321 [C]

FOR 452.subject: FOR
FOR 452.description: Explores prescribed fire in an ecological context and as a management tool. Emphasizes evaluating sites for prescribed fire potential/suitability, developing burn prescriptions and burn plans to meet landowner and ecological objectives, monitoring results, and accessing resources and expertise. Develops a burn plan and implements a prescribed burn.
FOR 452.prerequisites_raw: FOR 252 (may be taken concurrently) with C or better

FOR 456.subject: FOR
FOR 456.description: An introduction to the biological, physical, and sociological factors that shape the world's forests and the activities used to manage those forests. What influence these factors have on forest policies, practices, and outcomes. CROSSLISTED as FE 456 / FOR 456 .

FOR 457.subject: FOR
FOR 457.description: Use of linear programming, nonlinear programming, dynamic programming, and simulation to solve complex forest management problems, with emphasis on intertemporal multiple-use scheduling. Forestry transportation problems, multiple-use allocation, and investment analysis. Field trips required. CROSSLISTED as FE 457 / FOR 457 .
FOR 457.prerequisites_raw: FOR 329 with C or better and ( FOR 441 (may be taken concurrently) [C] or FOR 443 [C])

FOR 459.subject: FOR
FOR 459.course_name: FOREST MANAGEMENT PLANNING AND DESIGN I
FOR 459.description: Integration of environmental, economic, and social aspects of forestry in management planning. Development of strategic and tactical plans using diverse data types and sources. Senior capstone class projects. Lec/lab. CROSSLISTED as FE 459 / FOR 459 .
FOR 459.prerequisites_raw: FE 457 with C or better or FOR 457 with C or better

FOR 460.subject: FOR
FOR 460.description: Policy formulation and analysis for forest resources. Consideration of policy affecting land management approaches to planning, management, and social and economic development. Major forestry policy areas covered include outdoor recreation, range, timber, wilderness, and wildlife and fish.
attributes: CSWC – Core Ed - Writing Intensive Curriculum (WIC); CWIC – Bacc Core

FOR 461.subject: FOR
FOR 461.description: Explores tools and techniques for policy analysis, with an emphasis on policies impacting forest management. Uses case studies to demonstrate and practice using an analytic framework. Uses the model of an eightfold process to understand problem-solving and policy analysis in contemporary forest policy issues. Builds a multi-dimensional framework to analyze and evaluate trade-offs.

FOR 463.subject: FOR
FOR 463.description: Explores policy formulation and analysis of policies affecting land management, timber harvesting, and other forest practices on both private and public lands, particularly policies that address environmental concerns. Evaluates how regulations and policies evolve, including the role of public perceptions, forestry professionals, and other key policy players. Integrates writing appropriate in topic and style for natural resource professionals. CROSSLISTED as FE 463 / FOR 463 .
attributes: CSWC – Core Ed - Writing Intensive Curriculum (WIC); CWIC – Bacc Core

FOR 469.subject: FOR
FOR 469.course_name: FOREST MANAGEMENT PLANNING AND DESIGN II
FOR 469.description: A team-based, project-centric course for integrated timber harvest planning. Establish tactical and operational planning goals and constraints, identify feasible harvesting and transportation systems, and design harvest units to meet objectives and constraints. Lec/lab. CROSSLISTED as FE 469 / FOR 469 .
FOR 469.prerequisites_raw: FE 459 with C or better or FOR 459 with C or better

FOR 499.subject: FOR
FOR 499.description: Topics of current importance in forest resources issues, education, policies, economics, management, business, social values, silviculture, and biometrics. Topics will change from term to term. May be repeated with different topics for credit. Section 8: Social aspects of natural resource management (3 credits) graded.

FOR 513.subject: FOR
FOR 513.description: Analyzes effects of diseases on forest ecosystems. Focuses on recognition of important groups, prediction of pathogen responses to environmental changes, and management strategies for protection of forest resources. CROSSLISTED as BOT 513 / FOR 513 .

FOR 520.subject: FOR
FOR 520.description: Examines passive and active sensors used in remote sensing. Explores manipulation of geospatial data in R and classification of images using machine learning. Extract forest relevant information from lidar and photogrammetric point clouds. Sampling for accuracy assessment.
FOR 520.prerequisites_raw: FE 544 with C or better or GEOG 580 with C or better

FOR 522.subject: FOR
FOR 522.course_name: MODELING COMPETITION AND SITE INTERACTION EFFECTS ON SEEDLING PHYSIOLOGY, GROWTH AND SURVIVAL
FOR 522.description: Focuses on understanding and modeling the interactions between planted seedling physiology, site conditions and competing vegetation. Includes field trips to study sites, exposing the students to new advances in reforestation research and ecophysiological modeling, with a main emphasis on understanding the interactions between site conditions, conifer seedling physiology, and early-seral vegetation abundance and composition.

FOR 524.subject: FOR
FOR 524.description: Advanced topics in forest biometrics, including measurement of forest structure and dynamics, application of sampling theory and methods, and statistical techniques for interpreting forestry data.

FOR 525.subject: FOR
FOR 525.description: Develops forest models using regression and machine learning models. Explores techniques and assumptions used to develop static and dynamic models. Emphasizes regression analysis, random forests, and neural networks.
FOR 525.prerequisites_raw: ST 521 with C or better or ST 552 with C or better

FOR 526.subject: FOR
FOR 526.description: Focuses on the foundations and practical use of the process-based model 3-PG (Physiological Processes Predicting Growth). Utilizes output from the 3-PG model, which includes leaf area index, stand transpiration, stem biomass and volume, quadratic mean diameter, and basal area to evaluate site potential and analyze the effects of varying growing conditions or management actions.

FOR 528.subject: FOR
FOR 528.description: Conventions of written and oral communication in forestry and related disciplines including basic narrative development. Exploration of environmental, professional, and research ethics, and the role they play in effective communication with multiple stakeholders.

FOR 529.subject: FOR
FOR 529.description: Conduct field work carried out in Oregon to study forest dynamics. Understand forest stand development under normal and catastrophic conditions. Apply measurement techniques to evaluate the interaction between forest and human societies, with an emphasis on silviculture. Apply ecological theories and concepts to interpret the relationships among forest ecosystem components.

FOR 530.subject: FOR
FOR 530.description: Focuses on foundation of the sustainable forest management research. Topics include framing a testable research question, formulation of models, and hypotheses. Selection between Bayesian and Frequentist approaches to research. Emphasizes sustainability and its influence on decision-making in forest management, with example from forest certification, climate change, biodiversity conservation, and equity. Interprets and disseminates methods and results.

FOR 531.subject: FOR
FOR 531.course_name: ECONOMICS AND POLICY OF FOREST WILDLAND FIRE
FOR 531.description: Explores current issues in wildfire policy and management. Analyzes relevant laws and regulations, including liability standards and air quality rules. Uses an economic framework for evaluating allocation of resources, the role of incentives and risk preferences, and for valuation of forest assets under risk.

FOR 534.subject: FOR
FOR 534.description: Topics include optimal stand and forest management for timber production, economics of ecosystem services (e.g. recreation, biodiversity, carbon sequestration, water quality and regulation), non-market valuation methods, management under risk and uncertainty, discounting, intergenerational equity, sustainability, international trade and other global issues.

FOR 536.subject: FOR
FOR 536.description: Principles and applications of fire as a natural resource management tool; the role of fire in conservation management, restoration, and preservation of ecosystems. Covers basic techniques and current research used to describe fire behavior and spread, fuels and fuel manipulation, and fire effects on the biota. Focus will be on fire as a natural process in ecosystem dynamics.

FOR 538.subject: FOR
FOR 538.description: Emphasizes wildfire impacts to social and ecological values and conducts an assessment of wildfire risk to communities and wildlands. Explores mitigation opportunities from the built environment to wildlands, and how decision-makers use decision-support tools to prioritize actions. Identifies and critiques competing perspectives of risk, from defining the problem to implementing solutions. Applies gained knowledge to real-world examples to reinforce complexities of addressing wildfire risk.

FOR 543.subject: FOR
FOR 543.description: Manipulation of immature and mature forest stands for various resource management objectives. Principles and techniques involving vegetation control, thinning, fertilizing, and harvesting. Environmental considerations related to stand treatments. Two-day field trips required.

FOR 549.subject: FOR
FOR 549.course_name: SILVICULTURAL INFLUENCES ON FOREST ECOSYSTEM DYNAMICS
FOR 549.description: Analyze fundamental biological and ecological relationships driving ecosystem responses to silvicultural activities. Evaluate the implications of these relationships to the design of silvicultural regimes that achieve a diversity of forest ecosystem management objectives.
FOR 549.recommended: Undergraduate coursework in silviculture or forest ecology, and forest mensuration or vegetation sampling

FOR 550.subject: FOR
FOR 550.description: Sustainable forestry as part of the global sustainability movement. History of sustainability and its influence on decision-making in forest management. Current dimensions of sustainability: forest certification, climate change, role of environmental ethics, biodiversity conservation, maintenance of long-term site productivity, conservation of soil and water resources, roles of social institutions, and links to concerns for social justice.

FOR 552.subject: FOR
FOR 552.description: Explores prescribed fire in an ecological context and as a management tool. Emphasizes evaluating sites for prescribed fire potential/suitability, developing burn prescriptions and burn plans to meet landowner and ecological objectives, monitoring results, and accessing resources and expertise. Develops a burn plan and implements a prescribed burn.

FOR 561.subject: FOR
FOR 561.description: Explores tools and techniques for policy analysis, with an emphasis on policies impacting forest management. Uses case studies to demonstrate and practice using an analytic framework. Uses the model of an eightfold process to understand problem-solving and policy analysis in contemporary forest policy issues. Builds a multi-dimensional framework to analyze and evaluate trade-offs.

FOR 699.subject: FOR
FOR 699.description: Topics of current importance in forest resources issues, education, policies, economics, management, business, social values, silviculture, and biometrics. Topics will change from term to term. May be repeated with different topics for credit.

FR 111.subject: FR
FR 111.description: Develops speaking, listening, writing, and reading skills in French at the novice level through interactive and communicative activities, the study and practice of French grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation, as well as the exploration of cultural practices, products, and perspectives in the French-speaking world. Taught in French and English. Fluent users of the language are not permitted to enroll in this course.

FR 121.subject: FR
FR 121.course_name: SURVIVAL FRENCH FOR STUDENTS AND TRAVELERS
FR 121.description: Provides practical linguistic tools for short stays in France. Basic conversation skills, pronunciation, introduction to French non-verbal language, as well as cultural tools, introduction to French etiquette, visual dictionary, and tips for avoiding cross-cultural misunderstandings common between Americans and the French.

FR 211.subject: FR
FR 211.description: Builds on and expands students’ basic communication skills in French to progressively develop their speaking, listening, writing, and reading skills at the intermediate level through interactive and communicative activities; the study and practice of French grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation; extensive readings; as well as the exploration of cultural perspectives, practices, and products in the French-speaking world. Taught in French and English. Fluent users of the language are not permitted to enroll in this course.

FR 270H.subject: FR
FR 270H.course_name: *FRANCE TODAY: CULTURES WITHIN AND BEYOND ITS BORDERS
FR 270H.description: An exploratory study of French culture and society since 1945. Topics include: decolonization, immigration, Francophone intellectual currents, France's European vocation, and social conflict today. Conducted in English.
attributes: Western Culture; HNRS – Honors Course Designator

FR 311.subject: FR
FR 311.description: First course in the third-year sequence. Consolidates and expands writing, reading, listening, and speaking skills in French at the Intermediate level and above through authentic materials and interactions including short stories, news reports, and conversations with diverse fluent speakers and learners of French. Develops awareness of French-speaking cultures beyond France. Reviews grammatical structures and pronunciation rules. Conducted in French.
FR 311.prerequisites_raw: FR 213 with C- or better or placement test

FR 312.subject: FR
FR 312.description: Second course in the third-year sequence. Consolidates and expands writing, reading, listening, and speaking skills in French at the Intermediate level and above through authentic materials and interactions including short stories, news reports, and conversations with diverse fluent speakers and learners of French. Develops awareness of French-speaking cultures beyond France. Reviews grammatical structures and pronunciation rules. Conducted in French.
FR 312.prerequisites_raw: FR 311 with C- or better or placement test

FR 313.description: Third course in the third-year sequence. Consolidates and expands writing, reading, listening, and speaking skills in French at the Intermediate level and above through authentic materials and interactions including short stories, news reports, and conversations with diverse fluent speakers and learners of French. Develops awareness of French-speaking cultures beyond France. Reviews grammatical structures and pronunciation rules. Conducted in French.
FR 313.prerequisites_raw: FR 312 with C- or better or placement test

children.text: placement test

FR 315.subject: FR
FR 315.description: Develops job market skills in the field of French and international studies. Builds job market and career-specific vocabulary. Creates a professional portfolio by writing a cover letter, a curriculum vitae, by preparing for a job interview, through task-based activities and interactions. Uses technological tools and social media skills to enhance online career profile. Facilitates real-world professional scenarios through experiential learning opportunities. Taught in French.
attributes: CSC1 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Preparation; CSC2 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Engagement
FR 315.prerequisites_raw: FR 312 with C- or better and ( CORE 100 [D-] or CORE 300 [D-] or BA 100 [D-] or BA 300 [D-] or ED 100 [D-] or ED 300 [D-] or ENGR 110 [D-] or ENGR 110H [D-] or ENGR 310 [D-] or LA 100 [D-] or LA 300 [D-] or SCI 100 [D-] or SCI 300 [D-] or Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1)

children.text: Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1

FR 333.subject: FR
FR 333.course_name: *FRENCH CULTURE AND SOCIETY SINCE THE REVOLUTION
FR 333.description: Cultural life of the French people from 1789 to the present. Conducted in French.
attributes: Western Culture; LACH – Liberal Arts Humanities Core

FR 339.subject: FR
FR 339.description: Analyzes the francophone cultures and politics among French-speaking communities of the United States (such as Louisiana and New England), from the colonial era to the present. Investigates issues like minority status, marginalization, language and diglossia, women’s conditions, and migration. Applies theoretical approaches to diverse genres, including historical and contemporary texts, novels, poems, songs and documentary films. Examines types of systemic oppression within historical contexts and main course themes. Taught in French.
FR 339.recommended: Completion of a Difference, Power, and Oppression Foundations course

FR 340.subject: FR
FR 340.course_name: INTRODUCTION À LA LITTÉRATURE D'EXPRESSION FRANÇAISE: INTRODUCTION TO FRENCH LITERARY STUDIES
FR 340.description: Explores concepts and vocabulary fundamental to the study of French literature. Synthesizes the main currents of French literary history. Introduces French genres: prose, poetry, and drama. Applies techniques of literary analysis through close reading activities, discussions, peer collaborations and essay writing. Taught in French.

FR 344.subject: FR
FR 344.course_name: CULTURES FRANCOPHONES ET CINÉMA: FRANCOPHONE CINEMA
FR 344.description: Explores different cultures of France and the Francophone world through film. Discover socio-historical, political, economic, and cultural contexts through the study of films from (and/or about) France, West Africa, Quebec, the Maghreb, Vietnam, and the Caribbean. Taught in French.

FR 379.subject: FR
FR 379.description: Supervised practicum for advanced students. Assignments as proctors or tutors in lower-division French courses. No more than 2 credits may be used to satisfy degree requirements for a major in French; may not be used to satisfy requirements for a minor in French.
FR 379.recommended: Completion of 12 upper-division credits in French, including FR 311 , FR 312 , FR 313 and FR 315 , with a minimum 3.0 GPA

FR 399.subject: FR
FR 399.description: May be repeated for credit when topic varies. Not offered every year.

FR 416.subject: FR
FR 416.course_name: LA SOCIÉTÉ FRANÇAISE CONTEMPORAINE: CONTEMPORARY FRENCH SOCIETY
FR 416.description: Explores aspects of contemporary French culture. Examines key aspects of identity and society in France by exploring perspectives on contemporary social issues. Applies various linguistic and analytical skills through written analysis, debates, and discussions. Taught in French.

FR 439.subject: FR
FR 439.description: Examines diverse discourse structures and genres. Reinforces reading and analytical skills using French (and Francophone) short literary and other cultural materials. Explores informal and formal writing in French. Taught in French.
attributes: CSWC – Core Ed - Writing Intensive Curriculum (WIC); CWIC – Bacc Core
FR 439.recommended: Courses with extensive writing and reading practice in French

FST 101.subject: FST
FST 101.description: For food science majors. Orientation and academic guidance toward career planning in food science and technology.

FST 202.subject: FST
FST 202.description: Explores careers in food and emphasizes experiential learning opportunities and actions that promote early career advancement. Leads to the creation of relevant tools for successful internship and job searches. Introduce basic business concepts and vocabulary for food scientists.
attributes: CSC1 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Preparation; CSC2 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Engagement
FST 202.prerequisites_raw: CORE 100 with D- or better or CORE 300 with D- or better or BA 100 with D- or better or BA 300 with D- or better or ED 100 with D- or better or ED 300 with D- or better or LA 100 with D- or better or LA 300 with D- or better or SCI 100 with D- or better or SCI 300 with D- or better or ENGR 110 with D- or better or ENGR 110H with D- or better or ENGR 310 with D- or better or Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1

children.text: Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1

FST 212.subject: FST
FST 212.description: Methods of processing and preserving milk and milk products and related unit operations.

FST 213.subject: FST
FST 213.description: Laboratory and field work to accompany FST 212 . Field trip required.

FST 251.subject: FST
FST 251.course_name: INTRODUCTION TO WINES, BEERS, AND SPIRITS
FST 251.description: A descriptive introduction to the history, science, sensory, economics, and societal aspects of alcoholic beverages.

FST 260.subject: FST
FST 260.course_name: *FOOD SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY IN WESTERN CULTURE
FST 260.description: Exploring the sciences and technologies of food processing and preservation within the context of their historical, current, and possible future influences on what we eat, the structure of our society, and our day-to-day lives.

FST 265.subject: FST
FST 265.description: Explores culture and religion as socially constructed categories that affect eating practices. Discusses the relationship between food, culture and religion; explores the cultural and religious differences in the USA and intersections of racism, discrimination and religious oppression. Discusses how halal food culture is socially constructed and promotes cultural diversity and inclusivity. Introduces the concept of Islamophobia and examines how it can affect communities and their food practices.

FST 273.subject: FST
FST 273.description: A study of wine throughout history, from its accidental discovery and refinement through today, with a focus on the profound role wine plays in agriculture, social rituals, human health, economics, and the ambivalent pursuit of pleasure.

FST 280.subject: FST
FST 280.description: Investigates different types of fermentation processes, related techniques, and products. Engages in laboratory activities on cider fermentation and sensory evaluation.
FST 280.prerequisites_raw: ( CH 221Z (may be taken concurrently) with C- or better or CH 221HZ (may be taken concurrently) with C- or better or CH 231 (may be taken concurrently) with C- or better or CH 231H (may be taken concurrently) with C- or better) and ( CH 227Z (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or CH 227HZ (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or CH 261 (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or CH 261H (may be taken concurrently) [C-])

FST 315.subject: FST
FST 315.description: Students will be working in one of the FST pilot plants (dairy, vegetables/fruit, brewing, wine making, distilling) and will be assisting with the manufacturing of foods or beverages. Students must have available blocks of time in their schedules to contribute significantly to a production run. Production schedules for each pilot plant will be determined in advance of registration for each term. Not all pilot plants will be available each term.

FST 327.subject: FST
FST 327.course_name: INTRODUCTION TO SUSTAINABLE FOOD PROCESSING AND MANUFACTURING
FST 327.description: Discusses principles and assessment of sustainable food processing and manufacturing. Develops concepts of sustainable food processing technologies and food manufacturing operations. Explores sustainable processing technologies for various food products.
FST 327.prerequisites_raw: ANS 251 with D or better or FST 212 with D or better or FST 280 with D or better

FST 360.subject: FST
FST 360.description: Principles, practices, and regulations governing and ensuring the microbiological safety of our food supply through risk assessment, surveillance, and intervention.
FST 360.prerequisites_raw: ( BI 221Z with D- or better or BI 221HZ with D- or better or BI 222Z with D- or better or BI 222HZ with D- or better or BI 223Z with D- or better or BI 223HZ with D- or better or BI 221 with D- or better or BI 221H with D- or better or BI 222 with D- or better or BI 222H with D- or better or BI 223 with D- or better or BI 223H with D- or better) and ( CH 121 [D-] or CH 121NL [D-] or CH 221Z [D-] or CH 221HZ [D-] or CH 231 [D-] or CH 231H [D-])

FST 365.subject: FST
FST 365.course_name: MICROBIAL LAB TECHNIQUES IN FOOD INDUSTRY
FST 365.description: Emphasizes the role of microorganisms associated with food safety and quality. Includes practical hands-on experiments for the detection and identification of food quality and safety-related microorganisms. Covers microbial tests currently used in the food industry.
FST 365.prerequisites_raw: FST 360 with D or better and ( MB 302 (may be taken concurrently) [D] or MB 302H (may be taken concurrently) [D])

FST 370.subject: FST
FST 370.description: Assists students in preparation for internships and employment in the food industry by introducing compliance with food safety regulations, HACCP, and audits.
FST 370.recommended: One year of chemistry and one year of biology.

FST 375.subject: FST
FST 375.description: Focuses on the total quality management for the food industry. Describes the role of quality assurance and quality control personnel as important functions within the food processing organizations. Establishes and assesses a food safety and quality system within a food processing organization based on the total quality management principles and risk-based thinking concept. Explains statistical process control tools and laboratory control concepts for food processing.

FST 385.subject: FST
FST 385.description: Guides students in the investigation and critical evaluation of literature on a topic of current interest in food or fermentation science, and the development of their ability to write concisely and with precision about technical subject matter in this discipline.
attributes: CSWC – Core Ed - Writing Intensive Curriculum (WIC); CWIC – Bacc Core
FST 385.prerequisites_raw: FST 360 with D- or better and (WR 121 [C-] or WR 121H [C-] or WR 121Z [C-] or WR 121HZ [C-]) and ( MB 302 (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or MB 302H (may be taken concurrently) [D-])
FST 385.recommended: Completion of Bacc Core Writing II requirement

FST 420.subject: FST
FST 420.description: Covers sensory techniques used in the evaluation of the taste, smell, texture, and appearance of foods as well as the evaluation of consumer acceptance. Examines methods for measuring sensory qualities, underlying psychological principles, and statistical methods for analyzing data.
FST 420.prerequisites_raw: ( ST 351 with C- or better or ST 411 with C- or better) and ( ST 352 (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or ST 412 (may be taken concurrently) [D-])
FST 420.recommended: Familiarity with z-test, t-test, ANOVA, and post-hoc tests

FST 421.subject: FST
FST 421.description: Covers statutes, regulations, agencies, and policies controlling the production, processing, distribution, marketing, and promotion of foods. Practices large and small group discussions which typically involve the analysis of specific court cases, specifically on the logic/validity of the legal reasoning of each of the litigants, as well as that of the court.
FST 421.recommended: General knowledge of the food industry

FST 422.subject: FST
FST 422.description: An integrated course applying theories of molecular reactivity to model food systems. Lectures focus on the molecular bases of chemical phenomena that dictate the behavior of foods. Laboratories and recitations provide opportunities for students to observe, manipulate, and explore model food systems. Emphasis on major food components (water, lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates) and their behavior under conditions of particular relevance to food processing.
FST 422.prerequisites_raw: ( BB 350 with D- or better or BB 450 with D- or better) and ( CH 332 [C-] or CH 332H [C-] or CH 336 [C-]) and ( MTH 228 (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or MTH 252Z (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or MTH 252HZ (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or MTH 252 (may be taken concurrently) [D-] or MTH 252H (may be taken concurrently) [D-])

FST 423.subject: FST
FST 423.description: An integrated laboratory/lecture course covering methods used for the quantitative analysis of the chemical composition of foods and agricultural products.

FST 425.subject: FST
FST 425.description: The chemistry of food components in real-world food systems. Focused on water, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and food polymers, their interactions, and the effects of food processing and storage. Integrates writing as a learning tool and means of professional communication.

FST 428.subject: FST
FST 428.description: Emphasizes sensory techniques used in the evaluation of the taste, smell, texture, and appearance of foods as well as the evaluation of consumer acceptance. This includes methods for measuring sensory qualities, statistical methods for analyzing data, and proper interpretation of these results. Focuses on sample presentation, dealing with panelists, data recording, data analysis, interpretation of results, and report writing.
FST 428.prerequisites_raw: FST 420 (may be taken concurrently) with D- or better

FST 430.subject: FST
FST 430.description: Provides technical background and hand-on experience in food product development and food innovation.

FST 437.subject: FST
FST 437.course_name: CHEMISTRY AND BIOCHEMISTRY OF DISTILLED SPIRITS
FST 437.description: The underlying science of the production of the distilled spirits will be discussed systematically. The course will cover the requirements for water, the major raw materials (eg. cereals, fruits, agave, syrups, and woods for maturation) and the conversion of these into fermentable extract. The scientific principles of fermentation will be explored, in the context of both ethanol and secondary metabolite production. Distillation will be considered, in terms of the physics and chemistry of liquid-liquid separations, before discussing post-fermentation options such as blending, maturation and product finishing.
FST 437.prerequisites_raw: ( BI 205 with C- or better or BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( CH 331 [C-] or CH 331H [C-]) and ( CH 332 [C-] or CH 332H [C-]) and ( MB 302 (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or MB 302H (may be taken concurrently) [C-])

FST 439.subject: FST
FST 439.course_name: PRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS OF DISTILLED SPIRITS
FST 439.description: Compares and contrasts different approaches to the manufacture of distilled spirits by using some of the major spirit categories as examples. Discusses the management of a distilled spirits production plant in terms of legislative, safety and process/ product quality before explicit consideration of the requirements for establishing a distilled spirits production plant. Provides students with a broad understanding of the distilled spirits sector.

FST 440.subject: FST
FST 440.course_name: PRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS OF DISTILLED SPIRITS LABORATORY
FST 440.description: Building on the corequisite lecture course, the laboratory sessions focus on the essential analyses required in most if not all distillery operations and the production of final spirit products as examples of different spirit sectors. Provides students with a broad understanding of the distilled spirits sector and complements the lecture-based classes.

FST 455.subject: FST
FST 455.description: Focus on traditional regional recipes, explore and document how global change has affected food production and demand until today and how projected climate change will affect it in the future by analyzing the ingredient lists. Focus on one recipe/ingredient, find maps of past/current crop ranges, document changes, establish the carbon footprint, and identify possible replacement ingredients projecting future culinary solutions.

FST 460.subject: FST
FST 460.description: Explores the chemistry, biochemistry, microbiology and engineering of malting and brewing operations for the production of beer, including the compositional analysis of barley, malt, hops, water, and beer and their effects on beer quality.
FST 460.prerequisites_raw: ( BI 205 with C- or better or BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( CH 331 [C-] or CH 331H [C-]) and ( CH 332 [C-] or CH 332H [C-]) and ( MB 302 (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or MB 302H (may be taken concurrently) [C-])

FST 463.subject: FST
FST 463.description: Examines chemical, microbiological, physical, and sensory analyses for assessing beer quality. Focuses on analytical techniques used in the brewing industry to evaluate the quality of raw materials, wort, and finished beer. Explores industry-recognized standard methods and instrumentation interpret the analytical data to assess beer or raw material product quality.

FST 464.subject: FST
FST 464.course_name: PRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS OF BEER LABORATORY
FST 464.description: Focuses on hands-on instruction of brewery operations and analytical techniques for producing and assessing beer. Covers the sequence and purpose of key steps involved in producing beer while applying industry-relevant practices. Emphasizes analytical data evaluation and using results to inform brewing decisions and quality control. Provides training to produce a beer that meets commercially acceptable quality standards.

FST 466.subject: FST
FST 466.description: Explores principles of wine production technology from grape berry development through bottling, covering the microbiology and chemistry and biochemistry of fermentation, aging and production practices of red and white table wines as well as sparkling and dessert wines.
FST 466.prerequisites_raw: ( BI 205 with C- or better or BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( CH 331 [C-] or CH 331H [C-]) and ( CH 332 [C-] or CH 332H [C-]) and ( MB 302 (may be taken concurrently) [C-] or MB 302H (may be taken concurrently) [C-])

FST 469.subject: FST
FST 469.description: Examines the fundamentals of red and white wine production including procedures and equipment used and application of key chemical, microbial, and sensory analysis techniques to assess wine. Emphasizes the application of chemical, microbial, and sensory analysis techniques in wine production. Provides training to interpret analytical data from grapes and wine to make informed adjustments to winemaking practices.

FST 470.subject: FST
FST 470.course_name: PRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS OF WINE LABORATORY
FST 470.description: Focuses on the production of red and white wine and the key analytical techniques utilized in the wine industry (chemical, microbiological, and sensorial) during the production of wine.

FST 472.subject: FST
FST 472.description: Covers fundamental engineering principles for scientists and non-process engineers. Explores unit conversion, mass and energy balances, heat transfer, thermal processing, and lethality. Directed at food scientists and other majors who need or would like a working knowledge of food engineering principles.
FST 472.prerequisites_raw: ( MTH 227 with C- or better or MTH 251Z with C- or better or MTH 251HZ with C- or better or MTH 251 with C- or better or MTH 251H with C- or better) and ( PH 201 [C-] or PH 211 [C-] or PH 211H [C-]) and FST 360 [D-]

FST 473.subject: FST
FST 473.description: Covers fundamental engineering principles for scientists and non-process engineers. Explores mass transfer, extrusion, filtration, osmosis, distillation, extraction, drying, and freezing.

FST 479.subject: FST
FST 479.description: Introduction to fermentation microbiology that emphasizes the evolution of key physiological traits and biochemical pathways within key microbial genera. Explores the microbial ecology of processes used to make alcoholic beverages, food ingredients, and fermented foods. CROSSLISTED as FST 479 / MB 479 .
FST 479.prerequisites_raw: ( BB 350 with D- or better or BB 450 with D- or better) and ( MB 302 [D-] or MB 302H [D-])

FST 495.subject: FST
FST 495.description: Integrates food packaging science, biopolymer engineering, and pilot-scale packaging operations within a design-oriented learning framework. Explores the development and optimization of polysaccharide-based edible films intended for highly oxidative food products. Emphasizes structure-property-performance relationships, particularly the influence of formulation variables on mechanical strength, sealability, and barrier performance. Provides hands-on laboratory training to cast and characterize edible films, measure mechanical and barrier-related properties, and integrate materials into functional packaging configurations.
FST 495.prerequisites_raw: (MTH 111 with C- or better or MTH 111Z with C- or better) and PH 201 [C-] and CH 331 [C-]

FST 573.description: Covers fundamental engineering principles for scientists and non-process engineers. Explores mass transfer, extrusion, filtration, osmosis, distillation, extraction, drying, and freezing.

FST 574.subject: FST
FST 574.description: Examines the fundamentals of wine production including grape and wine composition, key winemaking steps, and regulatory compliance.

FST 575.subject: FST
FST 575.description: Explores wine etiquette and appreciation as a wine drinker. Examine major old and new wine regions of the world, analyze wine labels. Practice the use of sensory descriptors that are associated with major wine varieties, wine glasses, and the proper way to taste/order wine. Describe wine spoilage.

FST 579.subject: FST
FST 579.description: Introduction to fermentation microbiology that emphasizes the evolution of key physiological traits and biochemical pathways within key microbial genera. Explores the microbial ecology of processes used to make alcoholic beverages, food ingredients, and fermented foods. CROSSLISTED as FST 579 / MB 579 .

FST 580.subject: FST
FST 580.description: Emphasizes hands-on learning in basic and advanced microbiology concepts of food analysis that are used across the industry. Develops competency in aseptic technique, media preparation, culture handling, isolation, identification, and confirmation approaches as well as routine quality assurance testing, monitoring fermentations, and process validations. Includes experimental planning, inoculum preparation, food processing, sample analysis, and data collection, analysis, and interpretation.

FST 595.subject: FST
FST 595.description: Integrates food packaging science, biopolymer engineering, and pilot-scale packaging operations within a design-oriented learning framework. Explores the development and optimization of polysaccharide-based edible films intended for highly oxidative food products. Emphasizes structure-property-performance relationships, particularly the influence of formulation variables on mechanical strength, sealability, and barrier performance. Provides hands-on laboratory training to cast and characterize edible films, measure mechanical and barrier-related properties, and integrate materials into functional packaging configurations.

FST 620.subject: FST
FST 620.description: Current and/or advanced subjects in human sensory science. Includes 1) topics in human flavor perception that covers human psychophysics, neuroscience, and related fields, and 2) sensory evaluation techniques and data handling methods that are advanced in nature. Different points of view regarding above topics will be discussed.

FST 628.subject: FST
FST 628.description: The definition of flavor, analytical methods in flavor chemistry, and mechanisms of odor interaction in food system will be discussed. In addition, an integrated approach will be used to study the flavor chemistry of economically-important agricultural products in the Pacific Northwest such as dairy products, fruits, and alcoholic beverages.

FST 639.subject: FST
FST 639.description: Investigates the theoretical principles and structure-function relationships of food macromolecules. The theoretical principles are related, where possible, to observable phenomena during thermal processing and storage of foods.
FST 639.recommended: ( FST 422 or FST 522 ) and ( FST 425 or FST 525 )

FST 641.subject: FST
FST 641.course_name: PROCESSING WHEAT AND OTHER SMALL GRAINS: A MOLECULAR VIEW
FST 641.description: Provides a fundamental overview of wheat and other cereals from the perspective of the molecular level events that are important in milling, baking, and other processes. Uses cereal processing (focused primarily on bread-making) as the vehicle for placing elements of food chemistry, food polymer science, physical chemistry, and rheology into the cohesive framework of a single food category. Students will experience how the sciences of chemistry, physics, engineering, microbiology, biochemistry, nutrition, etc. amalgamate in the production of the selected cereal products.

FST 666.subject: FST
FST 666.description: An in-depth investigation of advanced wine processing techniques and wine research, focusing on their impact on production and wine quality.
FST 666.prerequisites_raw: FST 566 with B or better and (FST 567 (may be taken concurrently) [B] or ( FST 569 (may be taken concurrently) [B] and FST 570 (may be taken concurrently) [B]))
FST 666.recommended: Viticulture course such as HORT 454 and good understanding of how vineyard practices influence grape quality

FST 679.subject: FST
FST 679.description: Explores microbial ecology and biochemical transformations relevant to selected fermentation systems. Emphasizes the application of microbiological and physico-chemical analyses as indicators for successful fermentation outcomes through hands-on experimentation. Develops critical thinking through reading of current literature to inform hypothesis generation and experimental design, and application of knowledge to evaluate the outcome of an intervention applied to selected fermentation systems.
FST 679.recommended: FST 479 / MB 479 or ( MB 302 and ( BB 350 or BB 450 ))

FW 107.subject: FW
FW 107.description: Information relevant to academic pathways and career planning in the fields of fisheries and wildlife.

FW 113.subject: FW
FW 113.course_name: INTRODUCTION TO MARINE LIFE IN THE SEA-MARINE BIRDS AND MAMMALS
FW 113.description: Introduces first- and second-year undergraduates, teachers and non-degree students to the breadth of marine science course offerings and research at Oregon State University’s Hatfield Marine Science Center located in Newport, Oregon. Using an experiential based format, students collect field data to better understand marine mammals (whales, dolphins and porpoises), seabirds, and their interactions with their environment.

FW 115.subject: FW
FW 115.description: Introduces safe, effective methods to study shark species and their complex behaviors. Introduces students to biology and ecology of sharks through field, laboratory, and lecture experiences. Focuses on the ecological roles that sharks play in our marine communities and adaptations that have allowed them to swim in our oceans for nearly 400 million years. Explores how scientists study sharks: demonstrating safe handling techniques, tagging methods, and behavioral classification. Critically reviews the narrative of sharks as a societal menace in popular media against the essential role sharks play in maintaining marine ecosystems.

FW 209.subject: FW
FW 209.course_name: +CAREER SKILLS IN FISHERIES, WILDLIFE, AND CONSERVATION SCIENCES
FW 209.description: Develops and practices the skills needed to search, apply, and attain internships and jobs in fisheries, wildlife, and conservation sciences. Focuses on building a career-ready resume and cover letter, mock interview practice, attendance and reflection of a career-relevant event, and a personalized plan for their career advancement.
attributes: CSC1 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Preparation; CSC2 – Core Ed - Beyond OSU Career Engagement
FW 209.prerequisites_raw: FW 107 with P or better and ( CORE 100 [D-] or CORE 300 [D-] or LA 100 [D-] or LA 300 [D-] or SCI 100 [D-] or SCI 300 [D-] or BA 100 [D-] or BA 300 [D-] or ED 100 [D-] or ED 300 [D-] or ENGR 110 [D-] or ENGR 110H [D-] or ENGR 310 [D-] or Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1)

children.text: Baccalaureate Core Student with a score of 1

FW 251.subject: FW
FW 251.course_name: PRINCIPLES OF FISH AND WILDLIFE CONSERVATION
FW 251.description: History of conservation and natural resource use; ecological principles, and social and economic limitations of conservation; principles and practices of wildlife and fisheries management; role of research in management.

FW 255.subject: FW
FW 255.course_name: FIELD SAMPLING OF FISH AND WILDLIFE
FW 255.description: Introduction to sampling populations and communities of vertebrate animals emphasizing sampling design, collection and management of data, and communication of results.
FW 255.recommended: WR 121Z and familiarity with personal computers

FW 289.subject: FW
FW 289.course_name: COMMUNICATION SKILLS FOR FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE PROFESSIONALS
FW 289.description: Introduces students to the theoretical and practical dimensions of interpersonal and public communication in a natural resource management field.

FW 301.subject: FW
FW 301.course_name: FIELD TECHNIQUES FOR MARINE MAMMAL CONSERVATION
FW 301.description: A laboratory and hands-on experience covering field techniques, computer software for data organization and analyses, and understanding the practical management conservation application.
FW 301.prerequisites_raw: BI 302 (may be taken concurrently) with D- or better or FW 302 (may be taken concurrently) with D- or better

FW 302.subject: FW
FW 302.course_name: BIOLOGY AND CONSERVATION OF MARINE MAMMALS
FW 302.description: Examines the biology of cetaceans, pinnipeds, and other marine mammals. Topics including general adaptations to a marine existence; systematics and biogeography; reproduction; diving physiology; communication and echolocation; feeding and migratory behavior; the role of genetics in conservation; current whaling regulations and marine mammal/human interactions.
FW 302.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [C-] or BI 222HZ [C-]) and ( BI 223Z [C-] or BI 223HZ [C-])) or ((BI 221 [C-] or BI 221H [C-]) and (BI 222 [C-] or BI 222H [C-]) and (BI 223 [C-] or BI 223H [C-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [C-] and BI 206 [C-])

FW 303.subject: FW
FW 303.course_name: SURVEY OF GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEMS IN NATURAL RESOURCE
FW 303.description: Concepts underlying geographic information systems, global positioning system, and remote sensing; application to management and research, data quality issues, and case studies. Not a lab/skills class.

FW 307.subject: FW
FW 307.description: Examine career alternatives, develop career goals, learn what knowledge, skills, and abilities are important for diverse careers in fisheries and wildlife conservation, and develop an academic and lifelong plan for achieving career goals. Intended to assist students in developing a specialization in fisheries and wildlife sciences.

FW 310.subject: FW
FW 310.description: Gain professional experience related to students’ desired career path, either by attending a multi-day conference or by gaining experiential learning related to their career goals within the fisheries, wildlife, and conservation sciences fields. Reflect on these experiences and learn how to leverage them into your next professional endeavors.
FW 310.recommended: Collaboration, leadership, and problem solving skills

FW 311.subject: FW
FW 311.description: Surveys the adaptations of birds to a diverse array of habitats. Examines origins, anatomy, reproductive strategies, migration, flight, behavior, physiology, nutrition, and conservation.
FW 311.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 312.subject: FW
FW 312.description: Describes the external anatomy of birds using scientific terminology. Evaluates the evolutionary relationships of birds using modern naming procedures, and identifies birds by sight and sound.
FW 312.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 315.subject: FW
FW 315.description: Surveys the diversity of biological adaptations of fishes. Explores physiological and zoogeographical adaptations, reproduction, evolution, cladogenesis, morphology, behavior, and genetics.
FW 315.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 316.subject: FW
FW 316.description: Analyzes phylogenetic diversity, evolution, and relationships of the world's fishes, with a particular focus on Oregon fishes. Identifies fishes through anatomical analysis and the use of keys. Introduces the comparative method, systematic theory, taxonomy, field collection and specimen curation.
FW 316.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 317.subject: FW
FW 317.description: Surveys the origins, evolution, and diversity of mammals, and their adaptations to diverse environments. Examines taxonomy, reproduction, sensory perception, physiology, life history, and behavior.
FW 317.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 318.subject: FW
FW 318.description: Explore the diversity of mammals in temperate North America, with a focus on species in Oregon. Use skull, dentition, and pelt characteristics to classify mammals to order, family, genus and species. Describe habitat, range, diet, physical characteristics, and systematic relationships of mammal species. Learn and apply scientific skills, concepts, and terminology of mammalian systematics.
FW 318.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 320.subject: FW
FW 320.description: Examines the principles and concepts of population dynamics related to fish and wildlife populations. Engages in methods of estimating abundance, mortality, sustainable harvest levels and extinction risk. Introduces hands-on modelling for population analysis in lecture and labs.
FW 320.prerequisites_raw: ( MTH 227 with D- or better or MTH 241 with D- or better or MTH 241H with D- or better or MTH 245 with D- or better or MTH 251Z with D- or better or MTH 251HZ with D- or better or MTH 251 with D- or better or MTH 251H with D- or better) and (( ( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-])) or ((BI 221 [C-] or BI 221H [C-]) and (BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and (BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-]))

FW 321.subject: FW
FW 321.description: Develops a strong understanding of the linkages between community and ecosystem ecology and applied management strategies. Expands upon theoretical concepts such as metapopulation theory and invasion biology, and relates them to real world management issues, such as reserve design. Explores how wildlife and fisheries populations fit into the broader ecology of the system for effective management of these species. Examines community and ecosystem theory and the management strategies and techniques borne from them to accurately and appropriately evaluate and conserve natural resources.
FW 321.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 323.subject: FW
FW 323.course_name: MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLES OF PACIFIC SALMON IN THE NORTHWEST
FW 323.description: Explores the nature of the salmon problem in the Northwest. Experts from diverse disciplines describe principles of salmon biology, habitat ecology and management, socioeconomics of direct and indirect users, and government policies.

FW 324.subject: FW
FW 324.description: Explores where seafood comes from, and how it gets to the plate. Investigates how productive the world’s oceans are, and whether they can continue to feed (and employ) the masses. Discusses how different cultures, ethnicities, and regions of the world rely upon food from the sea for their daily meals and the importance of seafood to the world's total global protein consumption. Explores the cultural, societal, economic, practical, and environmental features of the protein that feeds billions.
attributes: Contemporary Global Issues; CSSS – Core Ed - Seeking Solutions

FW 324H.subject: FW
FW 324H.description: Explores where seafood comes from, and how it gets to the plate. Investigates how productive the world’s oceans are, and whether they can continue to feed (and employ) the masses. Discusses how different cultures, ethnicities, and regions of the world rely upon food from the sea for their daily meals and the importance of seafood to the world's total global protein consumption. Explores the cultural, societal, economic, practical, and environmental features of the protein that feeds billions.
attributes: Contemporary Global Issues; CSSS – Core Ed - Seeking Solutions; HNRS – Honors Course Designator

FW 325.subject: FW
FW 325.course_name: +*SEEKING SOLUTIONS TO GLOBAL CRISES IN RESOURCE ECOLOGY
FW 325.description: Examines historical and contemporary implications of the burgeoning anthropogenic footprint on rates and patterns of global ecological change. Analyzes the various reasons why these changes (also called Wicked Problems) are difficult to solve. Explores the drivers and potential solutions to these changes in the context of cultural and political institutions.
attributes: Contemporary Global Issues; CSSS – Core Ed - Seeking Solutions

FW 326.subject: FW
FW 326.description: A comprehensive approach to watershed management, one that includes biophysical, socioeconomic, planning and education related topics. Intended for students interested in the sustainable management of natural resources.

FW 328.subject: FW
FW 328.description: Manual and chemical restraint methods are covered with an emphasis on darting equipment, animal and human safety, drug pharmacology and species specific recommendations.

FW 331.subject: FW
FW 331.course_name: ECOLOGY OF MARINE AND ESTUARINE BIRDS
FW 331.description: Explores the diversity of marine and estuarine birds: their life histories, foraging ecology, and their physiological and behavioral adaptations for the marine environment. Implements field and laboratory experiences to practice ornithological research methods including field observations, species identification, data visualization and interpretation, Discusses conservation concerns for marine and estuarine birds. Introduces topics in oceanography.
FW 331.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 340.subject: FW
FW 340.course_name: +*POWER AND JUSTICE IN U.S. NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
FW 340.description: Explores the role of systems of oppression in natural resource management in the U.S. from history to present. Emphasizes the roles of policies and social norms in creating structural inequities to land use, environmental governance, and engaging in the scientific process.
attributes: Difference/Power/Discrimination; CSDP – Core Ed - Advanced Difference
FW 340.recommended: Completion of a Difference, Power, and Oppression Foundations course

FW 341.subject: FW
FW 341.description: Introduction to the philosophy, purposes, and methods of enforcing natural resource laws, emphasizing fish and wildlife laws.

FW 342.subject: FW
FW 342.course_name: FISH AND WILDLIFE POLICY AND GOVERNANCE
FW 342.description: Examines historical and contemporary policy, law, and governance regarding fish and wildlife in the United States. Addresses key regulatory and procedural aspects essential for the conservation and management of fish and wildlife in both state and federal settings. Introduces and analyzes policy as a social process, exploring the various governance and planning processes that shape how fish and wildlife policies are developed, modified, and implemented.

FW 345.subject: FW
FW 345.description: Examines the impact of climate change on natural systems, and explores actions to mitigate (slow) or adapt to climate change. Integrates knowledge from natural and social sciences and explores other knowledge systems. Analyzes existing data to inform decision making in conservation planning. Explores the role that managers and researchers can play in mitigating and adapting to climate change.
FW 345.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 345H.subject: FW
FW 345H.description: Examines the impact of climate change on natural systems, and explores actions to mitigate (slow) or adapt to climate change. Integrates knowledge from natural and social sciences and explores other knowledge systems. Analyzes existing data to inform decision making in conservation planning. Explores the role that managers and researchers can play in mitigating and adapting to climate change.
FW 345H.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 350.subject: FW
FW 350.description: Examines the primary causes of biodiversity loss and explores strategies to communicate these issues effectively to diverse stakeholders. Includes group activities that explore interdisciplinary approaches to solving problems at the intersection of endangered species and society. Provides a general background on endangered species biology and the social and economic implications of legislation enacted to protect them.
attributes: CSSS – Core Ed - Seeking Solutions; CSST – Bacc Core

FW 366.subject: FW
FW 366.course_name: ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS IN FISH AND WILDLIFE
FW 366.description: Explores the field of ecotoxicology, linking the ecology of fish and wildlife with toxicology of environmental contaminants. Pairs introductory concepts with key case studies, focusing on studying, managing or conserving fish and wildlife populations.
FW 366.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 370.subject: FW
FW 370.description: Evaluates the effects of habitat loss, exploitation, and environmental change on the genetic composition of natural populations, and how these changes affect the viability of populations. Explores units that define populations to inform management decisions and maintain biological diversity among populations. Introduces the tools and techniques geneticists employ from population, quantitative and molecular genomics, as well as systematics and phylogenetics. Provides a foundation for the acquisition and interpretation of wildlife genetic data. Expands problem-solving and critical-thinking skills using genetic methodology.
FW 370.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 371.subject: FW
FW 371.description: Introduces fish physiology and the interactions between physiological systems in fishes and both natural and human-modified habitats and ecosystems. Describes key aspects of fish physiology, understand how to use physiology to define fish health, and consider how large environmental factors like climate change will influence fish health. Examples and case histories will emphasize marine, estuarine, and anadromous fishes.
FW 371.recommended: FW 315 or one year of introductory biology; critical thinking, problem solving, and synthesis skills

FW 391.subject: FW
FW 391.course_name: *RIDGE TO REEF: SUSTAINABLE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT IN PALAU
FW 391.description: How do small islands address issues of natural resource management, food security, and sustainability? What role do communities, governments, and non-profits play in addressing these issues? Can traditional ecological knowledge help solve these challenges? What about climate change on small Islands? The Republic of Palau will be our classroom. Students will work with and learn from fishers, farmers, community leaders, traditional chiefs, terrestrial and marine biologists, and policy makers. Key topics include food security/production, climate change adaptation, protected area management, biocultural conservation, sustainable forest management, watershed management, sustainable development, coral reef and fisheries management, biodiversity measurement methods and ecosystem restoration.

FW 415.subject: FW
FW 415.course_name: FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE LAW AND POLICY
FW 415.description: Provides students with an understanding of the key legal frameworks within which they will work to conserve fish and wildlife resources. Examines federal law and policy relating to allocation and conservation of fish and wildlife resources.
FW 415.recommended: PS 201 or other introductory political science course

FW 418.subject: FW
FW 418.description: Understand how an increasing human population increases pressure on fish and wildlife communities and resources within ecosystems. Examines the interactions between humans and animal species within urban areas and the effects of urbanization on species, communities, and ecosystems. Topics include conserving biodiversity, invasive species, human health and well-being, and urban planning.
FW 418.prerequisites_raw: BI 370 with D- or better or BI 370H with D- or better or FW 321 with D- or better

FW 419.subject: FW
FW 419.course_name: THE NATURAL HISTORY OF WHALES AND WHALING
FW 419.description: Addresses the natural history of whales as a unique example of adaptation in an evolutionary lineage, and the history of whaling as a general example of the failings of international resource management.
FW 419.prerequisites_raw: BI 370 with D- or better or BI 370H with D- or better or FW 321 with D- or better

FW 421.subject: FW
FW 421.description: Focuses on the background, theory, evolution, ecology, politics, and conservation of invasions by introduced species in aquatic environments.
FW 421.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 422.subject: FW
FW 422.description: Examination of US law and primary international law focused on fisheries management with coverage of regulation of other ocean resources including energy, marine mammals, endangered species, pollution, and protected areas. Final project is intended to provide students with hands-on exposure to real-world fisheries and ocean management issues.

FW 426.subject: FW
FW 426.description: Leverages student’s existing knowledge to complex coastal concerns providing exposure to diverse coastal ecosystems and stakeholder perspectives. Emphasizes experimental (participatory) learning by integrating lectures, group discussions, field activities, analyses of real-world datasets, and interaction with professionals in fields related to coastal ecology and resource management. Examines topics ranging from coastal forests to open oceans, linking science and management. Explores various venues of coastal ecology and topical issues affecting management of natural resources on the Oregon coast through immersive field excursions.

FW 427.subject: FW
FW 427.description: Examines the general principles of how wildlife diseases emerge, evolve, and spread. Explores the relationships between human society, environmental change, and wildlife disease. Emphasizes how global environmental change (e.g. climate change, land use change, globalization of travel and trade) affect disease dynamics and cross-species transmission. Covers disease examples of North American mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians.
FW 427.prerequisites_raw: (( BI 221Z with C- or better or BI 221HZ with C- or better or BI 221 with C- or better or BI 221H with C- or better) and ( BI 222Z [D-] or BI 222HZ [D-] or BI 222 [D-] or BI 222H [D-]) and ( BI 223Z [D-] or BI 223HZ [D-] or BI 223 [D-] or BI 223H [D-])) or ( BI 204 [C-] and BI 205 [D-] and BI 206 [D-])

FW 430.subject: FW
FW 430.description: Prepares students to manage the task loading associated with performing scientific work underwater through a combination of classroom, confined water, and open water training. Introduces the diver to basic techniques and equipment used in underwater data collection. Includes required field trips to dive in both freshwater and marine habitats (two single-day trips and one three-day trip).
FW 430.recommended: Cold water diving experience; experience with cold water exposure protection (drysuit, thick wetsuit, thick or dry gloves)

FW 432X.subject: FW
FW 432X.description: Focuses on understanding aquatic ecosystems from an environmental and societal viewpoint and highlight the role of intensive salmon production in Chile and Oregon. Examines the intersection of intensive salmon production with environmental and societal values in Chile and Oregon. Explores innovative, transdisciplinary solutions to ensure the management of sustainable aquatic systems, bringing enterprise into harmony with the environment and society.

FW 433.subject: FW
FW 433.description: Synthesizes the principles of population dynamics from the viewpoint of a resource manager. Focuses on populations structured by age, size, or over space, and considers both fisheries and wildlife management. Uses computer programming in the R language in the laboratory work to implement examples from lecture.
FW 433.prerequisites_raw: ( FW 320 with C or better or BI 483 with C or better) and (( MTH 227 with C or better and MTH 228 [C]) or ( MTH 251Z [C] or MTH 251HZ [C] or MTH 251 [C] or MTH 251H [C]) and ( MTH 252Z [C] or MTH 252HZ [C] or MTH 252 [C] or MTH 252H [C]))

FW 435.subject: FW
FW 435.description: Examines the relationships between agricultural production and fish and wildlife populations and communities. Explores the impacts of agricultural practices on fish and wildlife. Field trips required; transportation fee charged. OSU Ecampus students are not required to attend field trips.
attributes: CSWC – Core Ed - Writing Intensive Curriculum (WIC); CWIC – Bacc Core

FW 439.subject: FW
FW 439.course_name: ^HUMAN DIMENSIONS OF FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE MANAGEMENT
FW 439.description: Examines the human dimensions of fisheries and wildlife including economics, policy, communications, and management.
